svg.title: A VLAN number plan drawn as bands across the identifier space, with six rules and one worked mapping example
svg.desc: A band from VLAN 1 to 1005 divided into segments: VLAN 1 in red as unusable, 2 to 9 reserved, 10 to 99 data, 100 to 199 voice, 200 to 299 management, 300 to 899 reserved for growth, 900 to 999 for blackholing unused ports, and 1002 to 1005 to be avoided as legacy defaults. Six rules follow: one VLAN one purpose one subnet, size subnets by powers of two with headroom, reserve blocks instead of inserting numbers in the middle, keep management off VLAN 1, keep voice separate, and put unused ports in a blackhole VLAN. A worked example maps VLAN 110 to the third octet of the subnet, and a note explains that the number is an interface contract with the rest of the documentation.
svg.text: A VLAN plan is a numbering scheme for people: the switch does not care, your runbook does
Numbers are cheap to choose now and expensive to change later — pick the gaps on purpose
reserved
never
reserved
data
voice
management
growth, in blocks
blackhole
avoid
One VLAN, one purpose, one subnet
The third octet is the VLAN, so the address names its own subnet.
No VLAN spans two buildings; no subnet spans two VLANs.
Size by powers of two, with headroom
A /24 holds 254 hosts; provision one that fills 70% of it.
Growing it later means renumbering every host inside it.
Reserve blocks, never insert in the middle
Give a new building 60-69, not 15. The gap costs nothing today.
It prevents a renumbering project three years from now.
Management off VLAN 1
VLAN 1 is reachable from any user port by default. A dedicated
management VLAN plus a management ACL is the minimum.
Voice on its own VLAN
Separate tagging gives QoS trust boundaries and a place to apply
phone policy, and it survives a PC plugged into the phone port.
Unused ports into a blackhole VLAN
An unconfigured port sits in VLAN 1 with full reachability. Put it
in a blackhole VLAN and shut it; a cable then gets you nothing.
WORKED MAPPING
In a local VLAN design the same number can be reused per building, because the Layer 3 boundary keeps them apart;
the subnet is what must be unique.
The number is an interface contract with the documentation, the firewall rules, the monitoring labels and the voice team's spreadsheet.
VLAN 1 is a default, not a decision: everything unassigned lands there, including the port someone patched last Friday and forgot to configure.
Sixty minutes with a spreadsheet at the start of a project is the cheapest network documentation you will ever produce.
